note: Decomposes Annex III into core concepts and publishes VAIR, a machine readable vocabulary for AI risk assessment.
title: To Be High-Risk, or Not To Be: Semantic Specifications and Implications of the AI Act's High-Risk AI Applications and Harmonised Standards
journal: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency
explain_beginner: The European Union's AI Act singles out certain AI systems as high-risk, meaning they face the law's strictest requirements, things like recruitment tools, credit-scoring systems, or law enforcement systems. But the law's list of what counts as high-risk, in a section called Annex III, is written in broad legal language that can be read in different ways, making it hard for companies and regulators to agree on whether a specific product falls into that category. This paper asks whether that vague list can be turned into something more precise and checkable. The researchers broke the Annex III descriptions into five building blocks: domain, purpose, capability, who uses the system, and who is affected. They then built an open vocabulary called VAIR that organizations can use to check their AI systems against the law's categories, plus a companion tool that can automatically flag likely high-risk classifications. Separately, they checked whether existing international technical standards support compliance and found most sit behind costly paywalls and are not built to be formally certified against.
explain_business: Any company building or deploying AI systems that might fall under the EU AI Act's high-risk categories, such as tools used in employment, credit decisions, or law enforcement-adjacent contexts, faces a real classification problem today: the law's own criteria are broad enough that reasonable people can disagree on whether a given system is covered. This paper's practical contribution is an open, structured vocabulary, VAIR, and a companion tool that a compliance team could use to get a clearer, more consistent read on classification, as an alternative to relying purely on legal interpretation. Separately, and arguably more consequential for near-term planning, the paper finds that the ISO and IEC technical standards meant to help companies demonstrate compliance are largely paywalled and not built for formal certification, meaning smaller businesses cannot simply buy a standard and check a compliance box. The realistic takeaway is to budget for both the cost of accessing relevant standards and ongoing legal interpretation, rather than expecting a clean, off-the-shelf compliance pathway.
explain_practitioner: The paper undertakes a semantic formalization of the EU AI Act's Annex III high-risk criteria, extracting five core concepts, domain, purpose, capability, user type, and AI subject, whose combinations function as classification rules. From this the authors build VAIR (Vocabulary of AI Risks), a formal taxonomy using SKOS and FAIR data principles, with over 172 concept instances across five modules covering AI techniques, use-case purposes, risk sources, stakeholder roles, and relevant standards. They pair this with a SHACL-based tool meant to help automate flagging of likely high-risk classification. A separate strand runs a gap analysis of ISO and IEC standards against the Act's conformity requirements, finding the reviewed standards are behind paywalls, a barrier especially for smaller companies, and mostly guidance-level rather than certifiable. The authors state real scope limits: VAIR currently captures only subclass relationships, stakeholder input in building the vocabulary was incomplete, no governance process yet exists for evolving it, the tool cannot flag prohibited systems under Article 5, only high-risk ones, and liability across a multi-party AI supply chain remains unresolved.
